results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec
All 40 body units' summaries by the spec-blind outliner state the controlling idea of the spec paragraph they are aligned to (p01-p40); the three callouts are page format and match no spec paragraph.

The outliner marked four units as holding two ideas (Introduction ¶2, Where the Sources Disagree ¶2, What AI Changes Here ¶1, Checklist ¶2). In the first three the two halves are exactly the two clauses of the spec paragraph's own controlling idea (p02 claim plus route, p30 offers-not-instructions so least structure, p34 model independent of producer plus the Emerging observation). Checklist ¶2 opens with the two-sentence callback the spec's conclusion requires and then makes the hand-off of p40; the callback serves as the carry-over into the open questions. No unit carries an idea foreign to its spec paragraph.

Every unit serves the supporting claim its section declares: scene and behaviour units S2, four-elements and AI units S1, levers units S3, procedure and anti-pattern units S4, limits units S5, worked example S3 and S4. No orphan unit.

Each spec evidence item is present and tied to its point: the four tables are each introduced and read by adjacent prose, Figure 1 has a lead-in and a caption that states what it shows, and each of the three quotations (Meadows on boundaries, Meadows on substitution of elements, Morieux and Tollman on resisting clarity) is followed by what it means for the argument. Small departures from the evidence wording, not affecting the point: p03 omits 'one product manager' (she appears in the worked example), and Figure 1 omits the weekly product sync edge.

All 38 declared transitions are expressed at their boundary with the declared relationship (e.g. 'Because each team built its own part' cause_effect; 'Those words exist' problem_solution; 'None of this says that people are interchangeable' contrast; 'Against those four stand three things' contrast; 'As a result, no third incident' cause_effect). Two form notes that do not change the relationship: the scene section's transition is one sentence where the spec says paragraph, and p40's hand-off transition comes after the two callback sentences and not at the very start of the paragraph.

results.draft_locus: What a Redesign Can Change: Four Levers and Three Conditions ¶1
results.quote: The capacities are not a lever. They are what the levers place.
results.finding: Both flow readers could not tell what it means for levers to 'place' capacities; re-reading the paragraph did not settle it and nothing later returns to it, so both went on without understanding the sentence. The spec's p18 does not ask for this sentence; say plainly what is meant (for example, that the levers decide where attention, judgment and verification are spent) or drop it.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item 1 (rated a); flow reader A, item 1 (rated a)
results.waived_by: Author (Željko Obrenović), 2026-11-19, rule 'max two rounds per chapter': the unit was revised after round 2 to address this finding and was not re-checked by fresh readers.

results.draft_locus: Worked Example: The Two Calendars, Read Again ¶1
results.quote: the fix below makes ownership of the rules explicit and narrow, which fits, because one rule for all applications is separable work with a stable interface
results.finding: Both flow readers went back to the trade-off table of the previous section and stayed unsure why a rule that three applications depend on counts as 'separable' and not 'interdependent'; the sentence asserts it without showing it, and it judges the fix before the fix table has been shown. The order of sections is fine; the prose should show the four changes first and then say why the rule is separable (one rule in one place, consumed through a stable schema).
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item 2 (rated a); flow reader A, item 6 (second half rated a)
results.waived_by: Author (Željko Obrenović), 2026-11-19, rule 'max two rounds per chapter': the unit was revised after round 2 to address this finding and was not re-checked by fresh readers.

results.finding: Apart from the two failed points: both flow readers describe a problem-to-tool order built as a chain of dependencies (case, describe, explain, change, apply, qualify, re-apply, AI, summarize), which agrees with the declared problem_solution pattern and the prerequisite_order of four-elements, behaviour and levers; both say they would move no section and that the limits section belongs before the worked example. No section's position is unclear to either; the prose under 'Checklist' is house page format and both rate it (b).

No term blocks a reader. Attention, judgment and verification are used in the callouts, the lead and the table before their definitions, the draft says so ('defined a few paragraphs below') and both readers rate it (b) or less. The two senses of 'boundary' are separated explicitly. 'Unowned Interface' is a failure-pattern name defined on the linked failure-patterns page (one reader, b). Part numbers and the evidence labels are explained in the book's introduction, which the readers were not given.

Opens on a puzzling scenario (Corvane's failure repeating after the lead was replaced), bridges to the reader's own experience, then states the thesis and the route. None of placeholder, restated question, dictionary definition, dawn of man or book report.

The conclusion sorts what holds by how settled it is, gives the synthesis, a course of action and the callback; it does not open with 'in conclusion', adds no new subtopic (each bullet is from the body; the next chapter's question appears only as the hand-off), and does not end on a rephrased thesis alone.

Synthesis: 'the description and the levers are one tool used in two directions: the four elements say what is there, and the four levers say what can be changed. A problem located in an element points to the lever that moves it, or to a condition no lever reaches.' So-what: 'run these eight checks on it before you change a person, a reporting line or a headcount' and the last check, 'Say in advance what your change will leave untouched'.

'Corvane's review could not say what had stayed in place between its two incidents. You can now: an unowned rule, a missing interface, an unassigned decision and an incentive that rewarded each team's own roadmap.' This returns to the opening case and answers its question as the spec's callback requires.

From the introduction alone the cold reader predicted the nine steps in order (two incidents, four elements, why behaviour follows structure, levers and conditions, procedure for a complaint, misuses, where the metaphor stops, Corvane again, AI), which covers all seven roadmap promises and the body's section order, and stated the central claim as the thesis statement has it.

AC-1 cold reader: 'This is a problem of the interface lever', restated without motive as changes reaching dependent teams only after release; would look at 'whether any agreed channel for announcing changes exists between the mobile team and its consumers', whether it has an owner and whether consumers know it. Matches the expected answer: an interface problem, look at the interface and not at the team's attitude.

AC-2 (judged from the draft): each capacity is defined in one clause ('Attention is how much a team can hold in mind well enough to change it safely. Judgment is deciding with the relevant information at hand. Verification is knowing that what was built is correct and was worth building.'), deferral is stated ('This chapter only names them. [[flow-and-the-constraint]] treats each in full'), and no argument rests on them: the answer to the puzzle uses interconnections and goals, resources and constraints, and the one later claim about capacities is labeled Speculative and deferred to Part XI.

AC-5 (judged from the draft): 'A decision right is the agreed answer to three questions about a named kind of decision: who may make it, whose input they must take, and where the decision is written down. This working definition is enough for the next four parts.' and 'An incentive is whatever the organization visibly rewards: promotion, recognition, headcount, a leader's attention.' Both are usable before Parts VI and VII, to which the depth is deferred.

AC-3 (judged from the draft): the limit is stated ('A software component has no interests and no memory. A team has both, so a boundary or a decision right is an offer that people respond to, not an instruction they execute.') and so is what the metaphor does not explain ('The four levers set people's context and do not specify their actions'; such systems 'can be understood and redesigned without ever being controlled').

AC-4 (judged from the draft): every claim from Meadows names Thinking in Systems at first use and the concept (definition of a system, complexity at boundaries and missing information flows, constraint and growth, persistence under substitution, 'bounded rationality', 'seeking the wrong goal', limits of control); every claim from Morieux and Tollman names Six Simple Rules and the concept (goals, resources and constraints, 'adjustment cost', the first rule 'understand what your people do', 'the hard approach', a function per requirement). The body takes no claim from Larson; An Elegant Puzzle is named in Sources with its concept, as the spec's decision log intends.
